## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
Generation 0 tried many networks and recipes, and every one scored zero dev and zero training success. So the agent never learns to build at all, and the shape of the network is not shown to be the problem. One mechanism fits every failure, though it is untested: a "DONE trap". At the start the policy places bricks nearly at random. Most random bricks fill cells outside the target, so each placement loses reward, and pressing DONE (return 0) beats placing anything. DONE is a single logit shared by every state, so it learns much faster than the local skill of placing bricks correctly. The policy then settles on stopping early and stops exploring. Starting the DONE bias at -2 does not fix this, because DONE still learns quickly. This round slows down learning of the DONE logit by scaling its output, and varies the recipe and global context around that. If all three still score zero, the trap theory is weakened.

### Round 2
All 3 round-1 trials scored 0 dev and 0 train success, and so did all 84 trials in generation 0. Slowing the DONE logit (0.1 or 0.03 scale), adding a global broadcast, or running more samples did not help. So the early-DONE trap is not shown to be the cause. With every score at zero I cannot measure noise or rank ideas, so this round tests things neither generation has covered. (1) A recipe extreme: lr 3e-3, small updates of 1,024 samples so there are about 240 updates, gae_lambda 0.8 and gamma 0.9. This tests whether the number of gradient steps and short-horizon credit are the problem. (2) Standard PPO initialisation (orthogonal weights, policy outputs scaled by 0.01) on the unchanged starting network, so the starting policy is near uniform. (3) A head that keeps each footprint cell's features in their own slot instead of max/min/average pooling, plus coordinate channels, combined with ideas 1 and 2.

### Round 3
All 90 trials so far score 0, including 6 in this search, and training success is also 0. Seed noise is still unknown. None of these changed the result: slowing the DONE logit, broadcasting global context, more samples, many short updates at high lr, orthogonal init, or per-cell footprint heads. The agent is not learning at all. My working guess is that convolution with pooling cannot easily do the key lookup the task needs: the brick lands at the maximum column height under its footprint, so the network must read the target at that landing layer. That needs a multiplicative interaction between height and layer. No candidate has tried it directly. A second guess is that the action layout or DONE position does not match what this world uses. For that, I add a zero-initialised dense path from global features to every action logit. It is a cheap hedge that keeps the convolutional prior. The two remaining candidates both use the new bilinear head and differ only in the recipe.

### Round 4
All 9 trials in this search scored 0 dev success and 0 training success, as did all 84 in generation 0. So nothing can be ranked and seed noise is still unknown. The world may differ from its description in a way that blocks learning altogether. Changes to the network and to the recipe within the usual ranges (DONE scaling, orthogonal init, short or long credit, bilinear landing-layer heads, dense global hedges) all failed. This is the last round, so I am spending the trials on untested regions rather than on refining a best design that does not exist. The three tests are:
1. A very long credit horizon (gamma 0.995, lambda 0.98), in case reward in this world is sparser than described.
2. A very large sample count (n_envs 1024, 1 epoch, about 50 large updates of about 400k steps).
3. Normalised hidden layers with a high learning rate, for stable optimisation.
A nonzero score on any of these would point the next program in a direction.
